title: The merchant and the parrot
hookLine: a caged parrot learns freedom from a parrot who played dead (Masnavi 1)
tomorrow: a shepherd talks to God like a farmhand. right or wrong?

lines: TELL THEM I'M IN A CAGE.
cards: Escape rooms charge you money to get locked in and then work your way out. Rumi's parrot gets out of a real cage, and its trick is the strangest one in the Masnavi: it plays dead.
A merchant keeps a beautiful talking parrot. Before a trip to India, he asks what gift it wants. Only this, says the parrot: tell the parrots of India that I'm here, in a cage.

teach.b: In India, the merchant passes on the message. One wild parrot trembles and drops from the branch, lifeless. Back home, he tells his parrot, and his parrot drops too.
Grieving, he opens the cage and tosses it out.
It flies straight to a high branch.

teach.h: YOUR SWEET VOICE IS THE CAGE.
teach.b: That parrot in India sent me advice, it says: your sweet voice is what keeps you caged. Die to it. Sufis tie the story to a phrase: die before you die.
It's sometimes passed around as a saying of the Prophet, but hadith critics say it isn't in the reliable collections; it's a Sufi saying.
Its meaning is the parrot's: let the part of you that the cage feeds on die, and you're free.
Now, this week, on one string. Bury yourself: grow in the dark. Delay isn't refusal: delayed, not denied.
Your seeking is from Him: the wanting is His gift. When He opens a door: walk through. The reed: the longing is the song.
The grammarian and the boatman: can you swim? Six lines, and every one asks you to let a little of the self go quiet. Fame, impatience, pride, a closed door, a closed heart, a puffed-up mind.

how: Sufi teachers use the merchant and the parrot to teach letting the ego's attachments die; the phrase 'die before you die' is a Sufi saying, though hadith scholars say it isn't a sound hadith.

games.q: what does “the merchant and the parrot” mean?
o: giving up every plan and possession at once
a fear of death that keeps you from living
letting part of yourself die so you can be free

games.q: who did what — tap the pairs.

s: 'die before you die' is a sound hadith in al-Bukhari
it's a Sufi saying; hadith critics say it isn't in the reliable collections.
in the story, the merchant's parrot really dies
it plays dead, gets tossed out of the cage, and flies to a high branch.
the wild parrot's fall was a message to the caged one
your sweet voice is what keeps you caged. die to it.

games.q: your friend is known as 'the funny one.' lately she's exhausted from performing it in every room. what would the parrot do?
o: let the role die a little, and be free to be quiet sometimes.
keep performing; people love her for exactly that.
quit the friend group so nobody expects anything.
games.why: the parrot's sweet voice was what kept it caged. letting that part die, not the friendships, is what set it free.

practice: Make a loose fist, as if holding something you cling to: a plan, a title, a picture of how things must go. Sit with it held for a few breaths.
Then rest the hand open on your knee, palm up, and leave it there for the rest of the sit.

wordCard.voice: The merchant and the parrot: Rumi's caged bird that goes free by letting its singing self die.

orig.note: Arabic: die before you die; a Sufi saying, not found in the reliable hadith collections.

carryVoice: The parrot's line, for the week ahead: die before dying, and see what flies out of the cage. Three of Rumi's eight, and a week in the book.

sources.ref: Rumi, Masnavi, Book 1 (the merchant and the parrot)
'Die before you die' (mutu qabla an tamutu), a Sufi saying; hadith critics (e.g. Ibn Hajar, as reported in later works) say it is not established as a hadith
